welcome.hook: How does your phone find one contact among 1000 in a split second?
welcome.intro: It does not read the whole list from top to bottom. Every question it asks throws away half of what is left. A [[bst|binary search tree]] stores [[key|keys]] so that a [[search]] works exactly like that. This app gets you ready for the COS212 lecture on BSTs, and it assumes you have never seen a [[tree]] before.
welcome.reassurance: Nothing here is marked, and you can retry anything as often as you like. Your progress stays on this device.
welcome.minutes: About 30 to 40 minutes. You can stop and come back any time.

LO1.text: Name the parts of a tree ([[root]], [[parent]], [[child]], [[leaf]], [[subtree]]) on a diagram.

LO2.text: State the [[bst-rule|BST rule]] and decide whether a given tree obeys it.

LO3.text: Trace a BST [[search]] and list the [[node|nodes]] visited, for a key that is present and for one that is absent.

LO4.text: Predict how many [[comparison|comparisons]] a search needs in a given tree.

LO5.text: Explain how the shape of a tree ([[balanced]] or [[lopsided]]) changes the number of comparisons, and why [[insert|inserting]] keys in sorted order gives a lopsided tree.

LO6.text: Judge your own readiness for the lecture from the check results and choose what to revise.

terms.name: Root
terms.definition: The single [[node]] at the very top. It is the only node with no [[parent]], and every search starts here.

terms.name: Parent
terms.definition: The node directly above another node, joined to it by an [[edge]]. Here 30 is the parent of 20 and 40.

terms.name: Child
terms.definition: A node directly below another node. In a [[binary-tree|binary tree]] each node has at most two children: a left child and a right child.

terms.name: Leaf
terms.definition: A node with no children: the end of a branch. Here the leaves are 20, 40, 60 and 80.

terms.name: Subtree
terms.definition: A node together with everything below it, like a smaller tree inside the big one. The left subtree of 50 is 30 and all of its [[descendant|descendants]].

rule.statement: For **every** node, all keys in its **left** [[subtree]] are **smaller** than the node's key, and all keys in its **right** subtree are **larger**.
rule.whole: The rule covers whole subtrees, not just the direct children. A key deep down on the left of 50 must still be smaller than 50.

search.analogy: In higher-or-lower, a friend thinks of a number from 1 to 100. A smart first guess is 50: whatever the answer, half of the numbers are ruled out. A BST [[search]] does the same thing. Each [[node]] is a guess, and the answer tells you which half to keep.
rules: If the key equals the current node's [[key]], you have found it.
If the key is smaller, go to the left [[child]].
If the key is larger, go to the right child.
If you need to go somewhere that is an [[empty-spot|empty spot]], the key is not in the tree.
search.counting: We count one [[comparison]] for every node we visit. Reaching an empty spot costs nothing, because there is no key there to compare with.
